cards.prompt: When should a developer reach for the Agents SDK rather than the Client SDK?

options.text: When building an agent without implementing a custom tool loop
options.rationale: The Agents SDK wraps the execution engine, ReAct loop, built-in tools and subagents that Claude Code uses.

options.text: When the application needs direct access to the Messages API
options.rationale: That is the Client SDK. The Agents SDK sits at a higher level of abstraction.

options.text: When the agent must run inside Claude Code rather than standalone
options.rationale: The SDK exposes what Claude Code is built on; it does not require running inside it.

options.text: When token cost matters more than development speed
options.rationale: The trade being made is abstraction versus control, not cost versus speed.

cards.explanation: The Agents SDK wraps the execution engine, ReAct loop, built-in tools and subagents that Claude Code itself uses, which puts it a level above the Client SDK — the Client SDK gives a developer the core Messages API and leaves the loop to them. The stated use case is building an agent without implementing a custom tool loop.

citations.section: Use the Agents SDK when building an Agent without implementing a custom tool loop

cards.prompt: What does the "ReAct" in ReAct loop stand for?

options.text: Reason + Act — the loop reasons about an input, decides to call tools, then interprets the results
options.rationale: It is the core construct of how any agentic system works.

options.text: Retrieve + Action — the loop retrieves context before acting on it
options.rationale: Retrieval is RAG, a separate technique.

options.text: Recursive Activation — the loop calls itself until the task completes
options.rationale: Invented. The loop repeats, but the name is not about recursion.

options.text: React — it is named after the UI framework the first agent harness was written in
options.rationale: A tempting coincidence, but the term is Reason + Act.

cards.explanation: ReAct comes from Reason + Act, and the loop is also called the agentic loop. It is the core construct of every agentic system: reason about an input, decide whether tools are needed, call them, interpret the results, repeat. Every Agent session in the Agents SDK follows this cycle.

cards.prompt: At which stage of the ReAct loop can Hooks intercept, modify or block a tool call?

options.text: Call Tools — the stage where each returned `ToolUseBlock` is executed and results sent back
options.rationale: Hooks sit around tool execution, which is why `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` exist.

options.text: Receive Prompt — before the input reaches the Model
options.rationale: `UserPromptSubmit` fires around prompts, but tool interception happens at the Call Tools stage.

options.text: Evaluate and Respond — while the Model is deciding what to do
options.rationale: That stage is the Model's reasoning; there is nothing to intercept there yet.

options.text: Return Result — as the final answer leaves the SDK
options.rationale: By then the tool calls have already happened.

cards.explanation: The cycle is: receive the prompt (user prompt + system prompt + message history + tool definitions), evaluate and respond (answer or emit a `ToolUseBlock`), call tools, repeat until no `ToolUseBlock`s come back or the max-turns limit is reached, then return the result. Hooks intercept at the Call Tools stage — which is what `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` are for.

cards.prompt: Which are valid Hook trigger points in the Agents SDK? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `PreToolUse` — before a tool is called
options.rationale: The interception point for blocking or modifying a call.

options.text: `PostToolUse` — after a tool returns results
options.rationale: Where results can be validated or transformed.

options.text: `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop`
options.rationale: Before a subagent spawns and after it completes.

options.text: `PreCompact` — before the context window is compacted
options.rationale: A chance to act before history is condensed.

options.text: `PostModelResponse` — after the Model generates any content block
options.rationale: Invented. The trigger covering the end of generation is `Stop`.

options.text: `PreRequest` — before each HTTP request to the Claude API
options.rationale: Invented. Hooks are defined around loop events, not around individual HTTP requests.

cards.explanation: The trigger points are `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, and `PreCompact`. Hooks are literal function calls that run in the application process, which has a useful consequence: they do not consume context.

cards.prompt: Because Hooks run at defined points in the ReAct loop, their output consumes part of the agent's context window.

options.text: True
False

cards.explanation: Hooks run in the application process and do not consume context. That is what makes them suitable for guardrails and validation that would be wasteful as prompt instructions — the check happens in your code rather than by spending tokens asking the Model to remember a rule.

cards.prompt: A main Agent spawns a subagent normally (not with `fork`). What does the subagent receive? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A specialized System Prompt tailored for its subtask
options.rationale: One of only two things it starts with.

options.text: A list of the main Agent's tool definitions, or a subset specified in `tools`
options.rationale: Restricting the list reduces the chance of tool overload.

options.text: The main Agent's conversation history
options.rationale: It does not — a subagent essentially starts from a blank slate.

options.text: The main Agent's System Prompt
options.rationale: It gets its own specialized one instead.

options.text: Preloaded skill content
options.rationale: Not unless explicitly listed in `AgentDefinition.skills`.

cards.explanation: A subagent starts nearly empty: a specialized System Prompt and a tool list, and nothing else. It does not inherit the main Agent's conversation history, its System Prompt, or preloaded skill content unless skills are explicitly listed. `fork` is the exception — a subagent spawned with `fork` inherits the main Agent's System Prompt, entire conversation history and tools.

cards.prompt: A subagent needs the full conversation so far in order to continue the main Agent's work. How is it spawned?

options.text: With `fork`, which inherits the main Agent's System Prompt, entire conversation history and tools
options.rationale: The single exception to a subagent starting from a blank slate.

options.text: By passing the history into the subagent's `initialPrompt`
options.rationale: `initialPrompt` is an auto-submitted user message, and it is ignored when the Agent runs as a subagent.

options.text: By listing the parent in the subagent's `memory` scope
options.rationale: `memory` controls which CLAUDE.md and project memory scope is loaded, not conversation history.

options.text: By resuming it with the parent's `session_id`
options.rationale: Resuming restores a *subagent's own* previous history, using both its `session_id` and `agent_id`.

cards.explanation: `fork` is the exception to subagent isolation: a forked subagent inherits the main Agent's System Prompt, full conversation history and tools. Resuming is a different mechanism — it restores a subagent's own previous run, including its conversation history, tool calls and reasoning blocks, and requires capturing both the `session_id` and the `agent_id` first.

cards.prompt: Which statements about defining a subagent are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Omitting `tools` means the Agent inherits every tool available to subagents
options.rationale: Which is why explicitly narrowing the list is the defence against tool overload.

options.text: `disallowedTools` supports MCP-level patterns such as `mcp__server__*`
options.rationale: Useful for excluding a whole third-party server at once.

options.text: `background: True` runs the Agent as a non-blocking background task
options.rationale: As opposed to blocking until it completes.

options.text: A programmatically defined Agent takes precedence over a filesystem-based one
options.rationale: And programmatic definition is the recommended approach.

options.text: `initialPrompt` is submitted whether the Agent runs as the main Agent or as a subagent
options.rationale: It is an auto-submitted user message only when the Agent runs as the main Agent — it is ignored when spawned as a subagent.

options.text: Skills not listed in `skills` cannot be called by the Agent at all
options.rationale: `skills` controls what is *preloaded* into context. Unlisted skills can still be called.

cards.explanation: Subagents can be defined programmatically — the recommended route, and it wins over a filesystem definition in `.claude/agents` — or as Markdown files. The parameters worth remembering for their surprises are `tools` (omit it and everything is inherited), `skills` (controls preloading, not availability), and `initialPrompt` (ignored when running as a subagent). Including the `Agent` tool in `allowed_tools` auto-approves spawning subagents.

cards.prompt: Which built-in tools can the Agents SDK run in parallel?

options.text: Read-only tools such as `Read`, `Glob` and `Grep`
options.rationale: Tools that modify state run sequentially, and custom tools default to sequential.

options.text: All built-in tools, since the SDK manages concurrency
options.rationale: State-modifying tools like `Edit` and `Write` are run sequentially.

options.text: Only orchestration tools such as `Agent` and `Task Create`
options.rationale: Those spawn work but are not the category singled out for parallel execution.

options.text: Custom tools, because the developer controls their side effects
options.rationale: Custom tools default to running sequentially precisely because the SDK cannot know their side effects.

cards.explanation: Read-only tools (`Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`) can run in parallel, while tools that modify state (`Edit`, `Write`) run sequentially — and custom tools default to sequential, since the SDK has no way to know whether yours is safe to parallelise. The built-in set spans file operations, search, execution (`Bash`), web (`WebSearch`, `WebFetch`), discovery (`ToolSearch`), and orchestration (`Agent`, `Skill`, `AskUserQuestion`, task tracking).

cards.prompt: An agent has grown a large tool inventory and is starting to choose the wrong tool. Which built-in tool is designed to help?

options.text: `ToolSearch` — it finds and loads tools on demand instead of pre-loading them all
options.rationale: Fewer tools in context at once means fewer chances of tool overload.

options.text: `Agent` — spawning a subagent avoids the problem entirely
options.rationale: Restricting a subagent's tool list does reduce tool overload, but `Agent` spawns subagents rather than managing tool discovery.

options.text: `Skill` — skills replace tools once the inventory grows
options.rationale: Skills supply task-specific expertise; they are not a tool-discovery mechanism.

options.text: `AskUserQuestion` — the user picks the tool
options.rationale: That surfaces a decision to the user; it does not address the size of the tool inventory.

cards.explanation: `ToolSearch` is the discovery tool: it finds and loads tools on demand rather than pre-loading every one. That directly targets **Tool Overload** — the phenomenon where an agent has too many tools to choose from and the Model starts choosing badly, also called Tool Bloat or the tool choice selection problem.

cards.prompt: Which settings control how the ReAct loop runs? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `max_turns` / `maxTurns` — limits the number of Turns that call tools
options.rationale: `max_turns` in the Python SDK, `maxTurns` in the JavaScript SDK.

options.text: `max_budget_usd` — limits the cost a ReAct loop can run up
options.rationale: A spend ceiling on the loop.

options.text: `effort` — limits how much reasoning the Model does before responding
options.rationale: Valid values are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`.

options.text: `max_tokens_per_turn` — caps generation within each Turn
options.rationale: Invented as a loop control. `max_tokens` is a per-request Messages API parameter.

options.text: `temperature` — lowering it shortens the loop
options.rationale: Temperature controls randomness of output, not loop length.

cards.explanation: Three controls bound the loop and each bounds a different resource: `max_turns` bounds iterations, `max_budget_usd` bounds money, and `effort` bounds reasoning depth (`low` through `max`). A Turn is one full round trip — receive input, request tool calls, call tools, receive results — all of which happens before control returns from the SDK.

cards.prompt: Which capabilities does the Agents SDK provide out of the box? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A built-in MCP client handling connection lifecycle, authentication, tool discovery and invocation
options.rationale: So you don't implement the MCP handshake yourself.

options.text: A permissions engine providing configurable tool-level permissions and enforcement
options.rationale: Removes the need for custom authorization logic around tool execution.

options.text: Session management including saving, resuming and forking sessions
options.rationale: No custom session storage needed.

options.text: Loading skills, commands and memory from `.claude` and `~/.claude` directories
options.rationale: Discovery and loading come for free.

options.text: A vector database for retrieval-augmented generation
options.rationale: RAG storage is not part of the SDK — that is a separate architectural choice.

options.text: Automatic prompt evaluation and grading of the agent's outputs
options.rationale: Evaluation is a technique you implement, not an SDK capability.

cards.explanation: The SDK's capabilities are all about not rebuilding plumbing: built-in tools, lifecycle hooks, subagent orchestration, an MCP client, a permissions engine, session persistence (save/resume/fork), skills-commands-memory loading from `.claude` and `~/.claude`, and a plugin framework. Retrieval and evaluation stay your design decisions.

citations.section: The Agents SDK includes the following capabilities

cards.prompt: The `SendMessage` tool lets an Agent message another named Agent, including one running in a different session.

options.text: True
False

cards.explanation: `SendMessage` allows an Agent to send a message to any other named Agent, including Agents running in a different session. That cross-session reach is what makes it more than intra-loop coordination — it turns separately running agents into something addressable.

cards.prompt: What is "Tool Overload"?

options.text: An Agent has too many Tools to choose from and the Model starts making poor choices about which to use
options.rationale: Also called Tool Bloat or the tool choice selection problem.

options.text: Too many tools run in parallel and exhaust the host's resources
options.rationale: It is a reasoning problem, not a resource one.

options.text: A single tool is called repeatedly until the max-turns limit is hit
options.rationale: That is a loop bounded by `max_turns`, not tool overload.

options.text: Tool definitions consume so much context that the conversation history is compacted
options.rationale: Context pressure is a related consequence, but the definition is about choice quality.

cards.explanation: Tool Overload — also Tool Bloat, or the tool choice selection problem — is when an Agent has so many Tools that the Model begins choosing badly. Two mechanisms in the SDK address it: `ToolSearch` loads tools on demand rather than pre-loading them all, and restricting a subagent's `tools` list narrows what it has to choose between.

cards.prompt: At the Receive Prompt stage of the ReAct loop, what is sent to the Model for initial reasoning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The User Prompt
options.rationale: The request itself.

options.text: The System Prompt
options.rationale: The developer's standing instructions.

options.text: The Message History
options.rationale: Everything that has happened so far.

options.text: The Tool Definitions
options.rationale: So the Model knows what it can call.

options.text: The results of the previous run's tool calls only, to save context
options.rationale: The full history goes, not a summary of it — nothing is persisted server-side.

cards.explanation: Step one of the loop assembles four things: user prompt, system prompt, message history and tool definitions. That list is the same set a single stateless Request carries, which is the point — the SDK is managing the loop, but each iteration is still a complete self-contained call.

cards.prompt: What ends the repeat phase of the ReAct loop?

options.text: No `ToolUseBlock`s are returned, or the Max Turns limit is reached
options.rationale: Two exit conditions — task complete, or budget exhausted.

options.text: Only when no `ToolUseBlock`s are returned
options.rationale: That would let a loop run forever; `max_turns` is the backstop.

options.text: When a `Stop` hook fires
options.rationale: The `Stop` hook runs *after* the Model stops; it observes rather than causes termination.

options.text: When `max_budget_usd` is reached, which is the only hard limit
options.rationale: A cost limit exists, but the loop's own exit conditions are tool-use and turns.

cards.explanation: Steps 2 and 3 — evaluate and respond, then call tools — repeat until either no `ToolUseBlock`s come back or the Max Turns limit is reached, at which point the final result is returned. The two conditions are worth distinguishing: one means the agent finished, the other means it ran out of room, and only the first implies the answer is complete.

cards.prompt: All the steps of a Turn — receiving input, requesting tool calls, calling tools, receiving results — happen before control is returned from the SDK.

options.text: True
False

cards.explanation: A Turn is a complete round trip and the SDK does not hand control back mid-way through one. That is what makes `max_turns` a meaningful unit of budget — you are limiting whole cycles, not partial ones — and it is why hooks exist: if you need to intervene inside a Turn, `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` are the seams provided for it.

cards.prompt: Which are valid values for the `effort` setting? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `low`
options.rationale: The cheapest tier.

options.text: `medium`
options.rationale: The middle tier.

options.text: `high`
options.rationale: More reasoning.

options.text: `xhigh`
options.rationale: Beyond high.

options.text: `max`
options.rationale: The top tier.

options.text: `none`
options.rationale: Not a listed value — there is no way to disable reasoning through `effort`.

cards.explanation: `effort` limits how much reasoning the Model does before responding, across five levels: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. It is one of three loop controls, each bounding a different resource — `max_turns` bounds iterations, `max_budget_usd` bounds spend, and `effort` bounds reasoning depth.

cards.prompt: Which tool-to-category pairings from the built-in tools table are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: File Operations — `Read`, `Edit`, `Write`
options.rationale: Read, modify and create files.

options.text: Search — `Glob`, `Grep`
options.rationale: Find files by pattern, search contents by regex.

options.text: Execution — `Bash`
options.rationale: Run shell commands and scripts.

options.text: Web — `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`
options.rationale: Search, fetch and parse web pages.

options.text: Discovery — `Agent`
options.rationale: `Agent` is Orchestration. Discovery is `ToolSearch`.

options.text: Orchestration — `Grep`
options.rationale: `Grep` is Search. Orchestration covers `Agent`, `Skill`, `AskUserQuestion` and the task tools.

cards.explanation: The built-in tools group by what they touch: File Operations (`Read`, `Edit`, `Write`), Search (`Glob`, `Grep`), Execution (`Bash`), Web (`WebSearch`, `WebFetch`), Discovery (`ToolSearch`), and Orchestration (`Agent`, `Skill`, `AskUserQuestion`, task create/update). The categories matter because parallelism follows them — read-only tools can run concurrently, state-modifying ones cannot.

cards.prompt: Which arguments explicitly allow or deny specific built-in tools for a session?

options.text: `allowed_tools` and `disallowed_tools`
options.rationale: The explicit allow/deny lists.

options.text: `tools` and `skills`
options.rationale: `tools` is the subagent's tool list and `skills` controls skill preloading.

options.text: `permissionMode` alone
options.rationale: `permissionMode` selects a predefined rule set; it does not name individual tools.

options.text: `max_turns` and `effort`
options.rationale: Those are loop controls.

cards.explanation: `allowed_tools` and `disallowed_tools` explicitly permit or deny specific Tools. Including the `Agent` tool in `allowed_tools` has a particular effect worth remembering: it auto-approves spawning subagents, which is the difference between an agent that can delegate freely and one that stops to ask.

cards.prompt: When does the `UserPromptSubmit` hook fire?

options.text: After a prompt is sent — both User and Assistant prompts
options.rationale: Broader than the name suggests.

options.text: Only after a User message is submitted
options.rationale: The notes specify both User and Assistant.

options.text: Before the prompt reaches the Model, so it can be rewritten
options.rationale: It fires after the prompt is sent.

options.text: Once per session, when the first prompt is submitted
options.rationale: It is a per-prompt trigger.

cards.explanation: `UserPromptSubmit` fires after a prompt is sent, and covers both User and Assistant prompts despite the name. It sits alongside `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` (around tool execution), `Stop` (after the Model stops for any reason), `SubagentStart` / `SubagentStop`, and `PreCompact` (before the context window is compacted).

cards.prompt: When does the `Stop` hook fire?

options.text: After the Model generates a stop_sequence message block, or stops for any other reason
options.rationale: Any termination, not just a stop sequence.

options.text: Only when a custom stop sequence is encountered
options.rationale: That is one of several reasons it fires.

options.text: When `max_turns` is reached, to allow a graceful exit
options.rationale: Hitting max turns is one way to stop, but the hook is not specific to it.

options.text: Before the loop terminates, so the agent can continue
options.rationale: It fires after the Model stops; it observes rather than resumes.

cards.explanation: `Stop` is deliberately broad: it fires after the Model generates a stop_sequence block *or stops for any other reason*. That makes it the right place for cleanup or reporting that must happen however a session ends — a natural `end_turn`, a max-tokens cutoff, or a stop sequence.

cards.prompt: What does the `PreCompact` hook let you act on?

options.text: The moment before the context window is compacted
options.rationale: A chance to persist or summarise before history is condensed.

options.text: The moment before a tool's results are truncated
options.rationale: Compaction applies to the context window, not to individual tool results.

options.text: The moment before a subagent's history is discarded
options.rationale: Subagent lifecycle is `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop`.

options.text: The moment before the session is saved
options.rationale: Session persistence is handled by session management, not by this hook.

cards.explanation: `PreCompact` fires before the context window is compacted. It matters because compaction is lossy by design — a long session's history gets condensed — so this is the seam for writing anything important to durable storage first. It also pairs naturally with the multi-agent advice to keep state external to the agent process.

cards.prompt: Where can subagents be defined as files, and which definition wins in a conflict?

options.text: Markdown files in `.claude/agents`, but a programmatic definition takes precedence
options.rationale: Programmatic is also the recommended approach.

options.text: Markdown files in `.claude/skills`, with the filesystem winning
options.rationale: `.claude/skills` holds Skills; agents live in `.claude/agents`, and programmatic definitions win.

options.text: Only programmatically — there is no filesystem option
options.rationale: Markdown definitions in `.claude/agents` are supported.

options.text: In `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is also where memory scope is read from
options.rationale: That file is memory, read according to the `memory` parameter.

cards.explanation: Subagents can be defined programmatically — the recommended route — or as Markdown files in `.claude/agents`. When both exist, the programmatic definition takes precedence. Keep the `.claude` directories distinct: `agents` for subagent definitions, `skills` for skills, and `CLAUDE.md` for memory.

cards.prompt: An `AgentDefinition` sets `memory: project`. What does the Agent load?

options.text: User memory from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` plus the project memory directory
options.rationale: `project` is additive — it loads the user scope as well.

options.text: Only the project memory directory, excluding user memory
options.rationale: The notes describe `project` as *additionally* loading project memory.

options.text: Only `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
options.rationale: That is the `user` scope.

options.text: The repository's root `CLAUDE.md` and every nested one
options.rationale: Per-directory `CLAUDE.md` reading is how Code Review works, not how the `memory` parameter is scoped.

cards.explanation: The `memory` parameter has two scopes and they nest: `user` loads memory from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, while `project` *additionally* loads the project memory directory. So `project` is a superset of `user`, which matters when deciding whether a subagent should see your personal cross-project conventions as well as this repository's.

cards.prompt: Which are valid `permissionMode` values for an Agent? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `default`
options.rationale: The baseline rule set.

options.text: `acceptEdits`
options.rationale: Auto-approves edits.

options.text: `bypassPermissions`
options.rationale: The most permissive mode.

options.text: `plan`
options.rationale: Planning without acting.

options.text: `readOnly`
options.rationale: Not one of the six modes. Restricting to read-only behaviour is done with `tools` or `disallowedTools`.

options.text: `sandbox`
options.rationale: Not a permission mode — sandboxing is a Cowork feature (Protected Environments).

cards.explanation: The six modes are `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions` and `plan`. Each bundles a predefined set of rules, so choosing a mode is coarse-grained; naming specific tools through `tools`, `allowed_tools` or `disallowedTools` is how you get precision.

cards.prompt: What does setting `background: True` on an Agent definition do?

options.text: Runs the Agent as a non-blocking background task
options.rationale: The caller does not wait for it.

options.text: Runs the Agent with reduced reasoning effort to save cost
options.rationale: That is `effort`.

options.text: Defers the Agent until the parent's loop completes
options.rationale: Non-blocking means concurrent, not deferred.

options.text: Suppresses the Agent's output unless it fails
options.rationale: It changes scheduling, not reporting.

cards.explanation: `background: True` runs the Agent as a non-blocking background task; `False` does not. This is the per-agent equivalent of the multi-agent guidance to run parallel subagents for speed — and it carries the same caveat, that parallelism needs more orchestration logic than a blocking call.

cards.prompt: A subagent must not touch any tool from a particular MCP server. What is the concise way to express that?

options.text: An MCP-level pattern in `disallowedTools`, e.g. `mcp__server__*`
options.rationale: Patterns let you exclude a whole server without listing its tools.

options.text: Omit the server from `mcpServers` and leave `disallowedTools` empty
options.rationale: A reasonable belt-and-braces move, but the feature being tested is pattern support in `disallowedTools`.

options.text: Set `permissionMode: plan` so no tools execute
options.rationale: That blocks all action, not one server.

options.text: List every tool from that server in `tools`
options.rationale: `tools` is an allow list — listing them would grant access, not remove it.

cards.explanation: `disallowedTools` supports MCP-level patterns such as `mcp__server__*`, so a whole third-party server can be excluded in one line rather than enumerating its tools — which matters because you do not control what tools that server adds in future. This is also the practical answer to tool overload from third-party MCPs whose descriptions you cannot improve.

cards.prompt: What must be captured before a subagent can be resumed, and what is restored? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The `session_id` and the `agent_id` must be captured first
options.rationale: Both identifiers are needed.

options.text: The session id is passed as the `resume` parameter in `query`
options.rationale: How the resume is requested.

options.text: The full conversation history is retained
options.rationale: Not a blank slate this time.

options.text: Previous tool calls and reasoning blocks are retained
options.rationale: Both are restored.

options.text: The parent Agent's conversation history is merged in
options.rationale: Resuming restores the *subagent's own* history; inheriting the parent's is what `fork` does.

cards.explanation: Resuming is the opposite of the usual blank-slate spawn: it restores the subagent's full conversation history, its previous tool calls and its reasoning blocks. It requires capturing both the `session_id` and the `agent_id` beforehand, with the session id passed as `resume` in `query`. Keep it distinct from `fork`, which inherits the *parent's* context rather than restoring the subagent's own.

cards.prompt: Which SDK capability removes the need to write your own discovery and loading logic for skills, commands and memory?

options.text: Skills, Commands & Memory — loading from the `.claude` and `~/.claude` directories
options.rationale: Discovery and loading are handled for you.

options.text: The Plugin Framework
options.rationale: That is for creating and integrating third-party plugins.

options.text: Session Management
options.rationale: That covers saving, resuming and forking sessions.

options.text: The Permissions Engine
options.rationale: That provides tool-level permissions and enforcement.

cards.explanation: The `Skills, Commands & Memory` capability handles storing and loading those three things from `.claude` and `~/.claude`, so you do not implement discovery yourself. The two-directory split is the same project-versus-personal distinction that governs skill scopes — repo conventions in `.claude`, cross-project utilities in `~/.claude`.

citations.section: The Agents SDK includes the following capabilities

cards.prompt: A developer adds a custom Tool that only reads data. How does the SDK schedule it by default?

options.text: Sequentially — custom Tools default to running sequentially regardless of what they do
options.rationale: The SDK cannot know a custom tool's side effects, so it assumes the worst.

options.text: In parallel, since read-only tools can run concurrently
options.rationale: That guarantee applies to the *built-in* read-only tools, which the SDK knows about.

options.text: In parallel only if declared with a read-only flag

options.text: It depends on the `permissionMode`

cards.explanation: Built-in read-only tools (`Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`) run in parallel and state-modifying ones (`Edit`, `Write`) run sequentially — the SDK knows which is which. A custom Tool is opaque to it, so it defaults to sequential. Being read-only in fact does not change the default; the SDK is being conservative about side effects it cannot inspect.
